questions.subtopic: Maximum HDB loan for short-lease resale flats
questions.principleTested: Maximum HDB loan for an older resale flat is pro-rated using remaining lease, youngest buyer age, lower of purchase price or valuation, and the 75% HDB loan limit.
questions.questionText: Cheryl is 34 and Axel is 44. They are buying a 4-room resale HDB with 40 years of lease left. Purchase price is $620,000 and valuation is $600,000. What is the maximum HDB loan they can receive for the flat?
questions.explanation: Use the lower of purchase price or valuation, which is $600,000. Then apply the short-lease HDB loan formula: ((remaining lease - 20) / (95 - youngest buyer age - 20)) x valuation limit x 75%. That gives ((40 - 20) / (95 - 34 - 20)) x 600000 x 75% = $219,512.
questions.plainEnglish: This is asking how much HDB will lend for an old resale flat with only 40 years left. Because the lease is short, you cannot simply take 75% of the value. You must first shrink the loan using the lease formula, then apply the 75% HDB loan cap.
questions.cavemanVersion: Old flat. Short lease. Use lower value. Use age 34. Formula first. Then x 75%.
questions.minimalVersion: Maximum HDB loan for a 40-year-lease flat with youngest buyer age 34 and value base $600k?
questions.memoryRule: Old lease, lower value, youngest age, then loan haircut.
questions.examShortcut: Short lease HDB loan = lease formula first, then x 75%.
questions.examTrap: Students either use the purchase price instead of the lower valuation, or they forget the short-lease adjustment and jump straight to 75% of value.

questions.subtopic: HDB resale grant calculation with short-lease pro-ration
questions.principleTested: Pro-rate CHG + EHG when the remaining lease cannot cover the youngest buyer to age 95; PHG is never pro-rated.
questions.questionText: Cheryl (SC, 34) and her husband Axel (SPR, 44) are first-time buyers purchasing a 4-room resale HDB flat with 40 years of lease remaining, located beside Cheryl's parents. Their combined household income is $8,000 per month. What is the total housing grant they can receive?
questions.explanation: CHG for an SC/SPR couple buying a 4-room resale flat is $70,000. EHG for $8,000 household income is $20,000. Subtotal $90,000. Because the 40-year lease cannot cover Cheryl (youngest buyer, 34) to age 95, CHG and EHG are pro-rated: (40 - 20) / (95 - 34 - 20) = 20/41 = 48.78%. $90,000 x 48.78% = $43,866. PHG ($20,000 for living near parents) is never pro-rated and is added in full: $43,866 + $20,000 = $63,866.
questions.plainEnglish: Cheryl and Axel are first-time buyers. Because one is SPR, their base grant is $70k not $80k. Their $8k income adds $20k more. That is $90k total. But the flat only has 40 years of lease left — it will not last until Cheryl turns 95. So the government cuts the CHG and EHG proportionally using a formula. One grant, the PHG for living near her parents, is never cut. Final answer: $63,866.
questions.cavemanVersion: Flat old. Lease short. Big grants get cut by formula. Near-mum grant never cut. Add together.
questions.minimalVersion: Pro-rate CHG + EHG using youngest buyer's age. PHG always added back in full.
questions.memoryRule: PHG never gets punished for a short lease. Everything else does.
questions.examShortcut: 1) CHG + EHG first. 2) Multiply by (lease - 20) / (95 - youngest age - 20). 3) Add PHG in full at the end — always.
questions.examTrap: Students who answer $90,000 calculated the grants correctly but never checked lease length against the youngest buyer's age. Students who answer $59,024 used the raw ratio 40/61 instead of the adjusted formula (40-20)/(95-34-20). And the formula uses the YOUNGEST buyer — plugging in Axel's 44 instead of Cheryl's 34 breaks everything.

questions.principleTested: A false statement of fact that induces the buyer can amount to misrepresentation, giving rescission and/or damages, without necessarily being fraudulent.
questions.questionText: Zed advertised a condo as 1400 sq ft and confirmed that figure to interested buyers. The title deed later showed the actual floor area was 1200 sq ft. Which of the statements is correct? (i) a misrepresentation is a false statement of fact made by Zed (ii) Zed has committed fraudulent misrepresentation (iii) the misrepresentation renders the Sales and Purchase agreement voidable / allows rescission (iv) the buyer can claim damages
questions.explanation: The correct set is (i), (iii), and (iv). Floor area is a statement of fact, not opinion. The buyers relied on it and paid the option fee, so this is misrepresentation and the buyers may rescind the contract and/or claim damages. It is not automatically fraudulent just because the statement was wrong; fraud needs dishonesty or knowing or reckless falsehood.
questions.plainEnglish: The agent said the condo was 1400 sq ft, and repeated it when the buyers asked. Later they found out it was only 1200 sq ft. Because they relied on that false fact when deciding to buy, this is misrepresentation. They may be able to cancel the deal or claim damages. But it is not automatically fraud.
questions.cavemanVersion: Agent said 1400. Real size 1200. Buyer relied. Misrepresentation. Can cancel or claim money. Not always fraud.
questions.minimalVersion: False floor-area fact induced the buyer. Misrepresentation with remedies, but not necessarily fraud.
questions.memoryRule: False fact plus buyer relied equals misrepresentation. Wrong does not automatically mean fraud.
questions.examShortcut: See false statement of fact plus reliance? Think misrepresentation first, fraud only if dishonesty is shown.
questions.examTrap: Students see a wrong statement and jump straight to fraud. The real distinction is whether the statement was just false and relied on, or knowingly or recklessly false.
